criterion: Role-based access control enforced for all Record endpoints
supabase_justification: Verified via automated pytest suite (test_authorization.py, 12/12 passing, Section 5) confirming org-scoped RLS policies block cross-org access on list/create/read/update paths.
django_justification: Same pytest suite plus 4/4 Django unit tests; permission classes + get_queryset() filtering enforce org scoping on all endpoints.

criterion: Passwords/credentials never logged or exposed in API responses
supabase_justification: Every sign-in/token response returned only access/refresh tokens throughout this build, never the password itself. Auth logs are only visible via Dashboard > Logs > Auth on a hosted project, not scriptable via CLI — noted as a visibility asymmetry, not treated as untestable.
django_justification: A deliberately wrong password submitted to /token/ does not appear anywhere in docker compose logs web afterward (Section 7 hands-on check, 2026-08-15, using the corrected -f django-variant/docker-compose.yml target). Response bodies also never echo the submitted password.

criterion: Data can be exported in a non-proprietary format without provider tooling
supabase_justification: Both variants are plain PostgreSQL (see row 77); pg_dump against Supabase's exposed connection string (Settings > Database) produces a standard SQL dump, not a Supabase-specific export format, and requires no Supabase CLI.
django_justification: Vanilla postgres:16 container; pg_dump/pg_restore work with zero Django-specific tooling.

criterion: Underlying schema/business logic is inspectable and modifiable
supabase_justification: Schema and RLS policies are plain, version-controlled SQL migrations (row 74), fully inspectable/modifiable outside the dashboard. Auth and Storage configuration, however, were done via the dashboard in this build, not expressed as code — the same asymmetry noted at row 71.
django_justification: All business logic is plain Python (models/serializers/views/permissions) under version control; nothing is configured through a dashboard-only path.

criterion: File uploads validated for type and size before storage
supabase_justification: Uploading a .sh file to a bucket named 'uploads' returned 400, but the actual bucket name configured in §3.5 wasn't confirmed before this test — 400 is equally consistent with 'bucket not found' as with a real type-validation rejection. The criterion is therefore recorded as not verified rather than scored in either direction; Supabase's per-bucket MIME-type restriction is documented platform functionality, but documentation alone does not meet this catalog's hands-on standard for this criterion.
django_justification: django-variant/config/settings.py still has AWS_S3_ENDPOINT_URL, AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY as literal placeholder strings ('<key>', '<secret>', etc.) from §4.6 — file storage was never actually wired up with real credentials this session, so no upload endpoint is functional to test. This is a real, disclosed implementation gap, not a silent omission.

criterion: Database can be migrated without vendor-proprietary extensions
supabase_justification: Supabase's managed Postgres does install several platform extensions by default (pgsodium, pg_graphql, pg_net, wrappers, vault), but this project's actual schema (organisations/profiles/records/file_uploads, RLS via SECURITY DEFINER functions) uses none of them — confirmed in the schema-review finding at row 81. The schema itself is portable to any plain Postgres instance.
django_justification: Vanilla postgres:16 image, no extensions used beyond core PostgreSQL/Django ORM features.

criterion: CRUD operations on Records complete correctly for all defined fields
supabase_justification: POST with org_id, status, and a nested payload object returned 201 with every field correctly round-tripped: {id, org_id, created_by, status, payload, updated_at} (Section 7 hands-on check, 2026-08-15). Getting here also surfaced that org_id has no server-side default (unlike created_by, row 44) — an unauthenticated-looking 403 from a missing org_id is really a validation gap, not an auth failure, worth a note in Section 5.2 since the RLS error message doesn't distinguish the two.
django_justification: POST /records/ with title, status, and a nested payload object returned 201 with every submitted field correctly round-tripped in the response body (id, org, created_by, status, payload, updated_at) — confirmed via a direct create call, Section 7 hands-on check, 2026-08-15.

criterion: Reporting/aggregate query (report_view) returns results scoped to caller's organisation only
supabase_justification: Initial implementation leaked all orgs' rows because Postgres views execute as owner by default; fixed via ALTER VIEW ... SET (security_invoker = true), re-verified live (single scoped row returned instead of all 50).
django_justification: report_view is a plain Django queryset filtered by the caller's org via get_queryset(); scoping verified directly.

criterion: System behaves correctly at organisation-data boundary (no cross-org leakage) under concurrent writes
supabase_justification: Not stress-tested under literal simultaneous writes. Inferred from architecture: org_id is server-derived per request from the caller's own JWT (row 44) and RLS scopes every write independently — there is no shared mutable state (e.g. a counter or single row) between two different orgs' requests that concurrency could expose. Flagging this as an inference, not a measured result.
django_justification: Same reasoning: org is server-derived per request via perform_create()/get_queryset() (row 44), with no shared state between requests from different orgs. Not independently load-tested for race conditions.

criterion: API accepts and correctly processes the full documented set of query parameters/filters
supabase_justification: GET /rest/v1/records?status=eq.open returned only rows with status='open' (Section 7 hands-on check, 2026-08-15) — the filter is genuinely applied, not just accepted and ignored.
django_justification: GET /records/?status=open returned a mixed set including a status='pending' record alongside status='open' ones (Section 7 hands-on check, 2026-08-15) — the query param is silently ignored, not an error, just no filtering applied. Consistent with no filter backend (e.g. django-filter) being configured in this build.

criterion: Partial/incomplete request payloads are rejected with a clear validation error, not a 500
supabase_justification: POST with an empty body ({}) is correctly rejected (403), but via a raw RLS policy violation ('new row violates row-level security policy for table records', code 42501) rather than a clear field-level message like 'org_id is required.' Rejection behaviour is correct/secure, but the error is not developer-friendly — it exposes internal policy machinery instead of naming the missing field.
django_justification: POST /records/ with an empty body ({}) returned 201 Created, not a validation error — model defaults silently filled in (status='open', payload={}). Arguably worse than Supabase's confusing-but-correct rejection: an empty/incomplete submission is accepted as if it were valid rather than rejected at all.

criterion: Duplicate/idempotent create requests are handled predictably (no silent duplication or corruption)
supabase_justification: Identical payloads (with org_id supplied) submitted twice both returned 201 Created (Section 7 hands-on check, 2026-08-15) — no idempotency-key mechanism exists here either; two separate records are created from one logically duplicate request.
django_justification: Identical POST bodies submitted twice both returned 201 Created (Section 7 hands-on check, 2026-08-15) — no idempotency-key mechanism exists, so two separate records are silently created from one logically duplicate request. Predictable (no corruption, no silent overwrite), but not deduplicated.

criterion: User-facing error messages do not leak internal schema/stack trace details
supabase_justification: POST with malformed JSON returned a clean PostgREST error: code PGRST102, message 'Empty or invalid json' (Section 7 hands-on check, 2026-08-15). No stack trace or internal detail leaked, though the message is terser/less specific than Django's (no line/column pointer).
django_justification: POST with malformed JSON returned DRF's standard clean error: 'JSON parse error - Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 2 (char 1)' (Section 7 hands-on check, 2026-08-15). No stack trace, file path, or internal exception class name — just states what's wrong and where.

criterion: Median response time for a single-record read stays under 200ms at low concurrency (10 VUs)
supabase_justification: read-heavy profile at 10 VUs, 3 reps: median 219-228 ms (results/supabase_read-heavy_10_rep{1,2,3}.json, Run 3, benchmarked 2026-09-03). Above the 200 ms threshold in every repetition, though only marginally. Two caveats are recorded rather than used to soften the score: the read-heavy profile is a list call over the 2,000-record baseline, not a literal isolated single-record GET, so it is a pessimistic proxy; and 25.8 ms of the measured figure is round-trip network time from the load generator to the London region (results/rtt_measurement.txt). Supersedes an earlier Satisfied score of 106.5-150.7 ms taken from a discarded run (results/BENCHMARK_RUN_NOTES.md).
django_justification: read-heavy profile at 10 VUs, 3 reps: median 296-304 ms (results/django_read-heavy_10_rep{1,2,3}.json, Run 3, benchmarked 2026-09-03), roughly 50 percent over the threshold. The same list-endpoint proxy caveat applies as for Supabase, and 58.9 ms is measured round-trip time to the Frankfurt VPS, 33 ms more than the Supabase path (results/rtt_measurement.txt). Supersedes an earlier Satisfied score of 39.0-55.8 ms, which was measured over loopback with no network path at all (results/BENCHMARK_RUN_NOTES.md).

criterion: p95 response time at moderate concurrency (50 VUs) stays under 2s for read-heavy workload
supabase_justification: read-heavy profile at 50 VUs, 3 reps: p95 2,561-2,676 ms (results/supabase_read-heavy_50_rep{1,2,3}.json, Run 3, benchmarked 2026-09-03), between 28 and 34 percent over the 2 s threshold in all three repetitions. PostgREST holds tail latency low on the write-heavy profile at the same concurrency (p95 452-723 ms) but not on the 2,000-record list read. Supersedes an earlier Satisfied score of 618-930 ms taken from a discarded run (results/BENCHMARK_RUN_NOTES.md).
django_justification: read-heavy profile at 50 VUs, 3 reps: p95 1,496-1,502 ms (results/django_read-heavy_50_rep{1,2,3}.json, Run 3, benchmarked 2026-09-03). Under the 2 s threshold in all three repetitions, with a 6 ms spread between them. Five synchronous Gunicorn workers are sufficient for this profile at this concurrency. Supersedes an earlier Not satisfied score of 13.25-13.83 s, which came from a sweep in which the record table grew roughly 545-fold mid-run while neither variant paginates its list endpoint (results/BENCHMARK_RUN_NOTES.md).

criterion: System degrades gracefully (errors, not silent data loss) under load beyond nominal capacity
supabase_justification: At 200 VUs, four times the nominal level, latency rose but the error rate stayed at or below 0.1 percent on all three profiles and no repetition reached the k6 timeout ceiling (results/table_5_1_summary_final.csv, Run 3, benchmarked 2026-09-03). Degradation is a latency curve rather than a failure cliff, and no data loss or corruption was observed in any run.
django_justification: At 200 VUs the error rate likewise stayed at or below 0.1 percent on all three profiles, with no timeouts (results/table_5_1_summary_final.csv, Run 3, benchmarked 2026-09-03). Upgraded from Partial: the earlier score recorded a 73 to 100 percent mixed-profile failure rate, but that result came from a sweep with no dataset reset, in which read latency tracked an unbounded and steadily growing table. It does not reproduce under the fixed 2,000-record protocol of Section 3.3 and is therefore not treated as evidence (results/BENCHMARK_RUN_NOTES.md).

criterion: Database connection pooling is present and configurable
supabase_justification: Supabase provides Supavisor, a connection pooler available on every project by default, with pool size and connection mode (transaction/session, ports 6543/5432) configurable from the Dashboard's Database settings (supabase.com/docs).
django_justification: Django connects directly via psycopg2 with no pooling layer configured in this build; Postgres connection pooling would require adding pgbouncer or a package like django-db-connection-pool, neither of which was set up.

criterion: N+1 query patterns are avoidable/avoided in the default data-access path for list endpoints
supabase_justification: PostgREST resolves embedded/related resources via a single SQL query with joins, not per-row follow-up queries — N+1 is structurally avoided at the API layer by design, not something the developer has to opt into.
django_justification: grep -n 'select_related|prefetch_related' core/views.py returned zero matches — no query-optimisation calls are used anywhere in the view layer. Any endpoint that serialises related objects (e.g. org membership) would issue one query per row by default.

criterion: Pagination is supported and enforced by default on list endpoints (no unbounded result sets)
supabase_justification: GET /rest/v1/records returns a Content-Range header (e.g. 0-999/*) and caps the response at 1000 rows by default (PostgREST's default max-rows), even with no explicit Range/limit param supplied by the client. Clients paginate further via the Range header.
django_justification: Confirmed via the SQL-injection probe response and a direct list call (Section 7 hands-on checks, 2026-08-14): GET /records/ returns the entire in-org record set (the full 2,000-record benchmark baseline) as a bare, unbounded JSON array — no Content-Range-equivalent metadata, no page/limit wrapper. DRF pagination classes were never configured.

criterion: API follows a documented, standard convention (REST/OpenAPI) that third-party HTTP clients can consume without custom SDKs
supabase_justification: Every request against Supabase throughout this build used plain curl (standard verb+path+JSON, Bearer/apikey headers), no SDK required; PostgREST also auto-generates a machine-readable OpenAPI spec at the API root.
django_justification: Every request against Django likewise used plain curl with no SDK, satisfying the 'consumable by standard HTTP clients' half of the criterion. But no machine-readable OpenAPI spec is generated — that would require adding drf-spectacular or drf-yasg, neither configured in this build.

criterion: System can coexist with other services sharing the same database/infrastructure without conflict
supabase_justification: Supabase officially exposes a direct Postgres connection string (Settings > Database) specifically so other tools (BI/analytics, ORMs, cron jobs) can connect to the same underlying database alongside the Supabase-managed API layer.
django_justification: The db container is a standard postgres:16 instance reachable by any other service on the same Docker network or via an exposed port; nothing about the schema or RLS-free setup prevents additional consumers.

criterion: Standard authentication tooling (e.g. Postman, curl, standard OAuth/JWT libraries) works against the API without provider-specific plugins
supabase_justification: Every authenticated request this session used plain curl with a standard Authorization: Bearer <JWT> header (plus Supabase's apikey header, a normal HTTP header, not a plugin) — no provider SDK was ever required.
django_justification: Same — plain curl with a standard Authorization: Bearer <JWT> header throughout; no custom tooling required.

criterion: Client libraries/SDKs are available in more than one language/ecosystem
supabase_justification: Official/community client libraries exist for JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Flutter/Dart, Swift, Kotlin, C#, Go, Ruby, and GDScript (supabase.com/docs/guides/api/rest/client-libs).
django_justification: No official generated client library ships with this implementation — it's a plain DRF REST API, consumable from any language's standard HTTP client, but nothing is officially provided or maintained the way Supabase's typed SDKs are.

criterion: API versioning strategy exists and is documented
supabase_justification: The REST endpoint is nominally versioned in its URL (/rest/v1/), but this reflects the platform's PostgREST version, not application-level API versioning. Supabase's documented recommendation for versioning your own schema/breaking changes is to use separate Postgres schemas (e.g. v1, v2) with postgrest-js's schema switch — a real strategy, but manual and not enforced by the platform.
django_justification: No versioning strategy (URL, header, or otherwise) was configured for this reference implementation; DRF supports several versioning schemes out of the box, but none was set up in this build.

criterion: Documentation/dashboard is understandable to a developer without prior platform-specific experience within a reasonable ramp-up (subjective, state your own ramp-up time)
supabase_justification: Self-reported by the developer: felt faster to get comfortable with, despite the RLS recursion incident requiring a genuine conceptual learning moment (SECURITY DEFINER functions, RLS evaluation order) before policies worked correctly.
django_justification: Self-reported: comparatively slower to reach comfort, consistent with the volume of hands-on troubleshooting this build required on the Django side (Gunicorn worker sizing, pytest/coverage setup, JWT-refresh flow, missing pagination/health endpoints).

criterion: Common administrative tasks (e.g. viewing a table's rows, checking a policy) are reachable within a small, countable number of clicks/commands
supabase_justification: Self-reported: 2-3 clicks from the dashboard homepage to view a table's rows (Table Editor > select table) or check a policy (Authentication > Policies > select table).
django_justification: No admin UI is configured in this build (row 30); the equivalent operation would be a psql or Django-shell command, not a comparable 'click count.'

criterion: Error messages returned to a developer/operator are actionable (state what's wrong and how to fix it)
supabase_justification: Same evidence as row 12: the empty-payload rejection returns a raw RLS policy violation ('new row violates row-level security policy for table records', code 42501) rather than naming the missing field — technically correct but not developer-friendly.
django_justification: Inconsistent rather than uniformly good or bad. Where an error IS returned, it's genuinely actionable: the malformed-JSON message ('JSON parse error - Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 2 (char 1)', confirmed via Section 7 hands-on check, 2026-08-15) states exactly what's wrong and where. But the empty-payload case (row 12) isn't an error at all — it silently accepts defaults instead of rejecting, which is arguably worse than an unhelpful message, since there's no message to act on in the first place.

criterion: Setup/onboarding requires no undocumented manual steps beyond what the platform's own quickstart describes
supabase_justification: Real undocumented steps were needed beyond the platform's own quickstart: the RLS recursion fix (SECURITY DEFINER pattern) and the security_invoker view fix (entry not in quickstart docs) both required troubleshooting beyond what Supabase's own getting-started guide covers.
django_justification: Real undocumented steps were needed beyond Django's own tutorial: Gunicorn worker sizing for a target compute budget (entry 7), installing pytest/pytest-cov inside the container, passing --ds=config.settings, and building a JWT-refresh flow — none of which are called out in Django's standard quickstart. Both variants score the same here, an interesting shared finding rather than a BaaS-vs-self-hosted differentiator (see Section 5.2 discussion).

criterion: Dashboard/admin UI is available out of the box without custom development
supabase_justification: Table Editor, Authentication, Storage, and SQL Editor are all available immediately on project creation, no setup required — used directly throughout this build (rows 3, 27).
django_justification: No admin UI is registered for these models in this build — Django's built-in admin site was never wired up to Organisation/UserAccount/Record/FileUpload. DRF's browsable API is dev-only (requires DEBUG=True) and wasn't confirmed enabled either; nothing dashboard-like is available out of the box as deployed.

criterion: Accessibility of any provided dashboard UI (keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels) meets a basic bar
supabase_justification: Self-reported spot-check (2026-08-15), with a specific finding rather than a blanket 'doesn't work': moving between different areas of the dashboard (sidebar sections, table list, panels) requires the mouse cursor — arrow-key/Tab navigation between these regions does not work. Inside the SQL Editor specifically, keyboard navigation of the code itself (arrow keys, standard text-editing shortcuts) works normally, since that component is a conventional code editor with its own internal keyboard handling. The gap is in cross-panel/global dashboard navigation, not in every widget individually — a more precise finding than 'keyboard navigation is broken.'
django_justification: No admin UI is available in this build to spot-check (row 30); the criterion doesn't apply.

criterion: System recovers automatically from a transient database connection loss without manual intervention
supabase_justification: Not independently testable (no ability to stop Supabase's underlying database); connection recovery is the platform's operational responsibility.
django_justification: db container stopped, a request during the outage correctly returned 500 (not a hang or corrupted response), db container restarted, and the very next request succeeded (200) with no web container restart needed (Section 7 hands-on check, 2026-08-15) — Django/psycopg2 re-established the connection automatically.

criterion: A crashed worker/process is automatically restarted without operator action
supabase_justification: Supabase's infrastructure (Postgres, PostgREST, GoTrue) is operated by the platform; a crashed process is the platform's operational responsibility, not something the project owner configures or observes directly.
django_justification: Confirmed via grep against django-variant/docker-compose.yml (Section 7 hands-on check, 2026-08-15): no restart: policy is set on any service. A crashed web or db container would stay down until an operator manually ran docker compose up again.

criterion: Data is durably persisted across a full restart of all application containers/services
supabase_justification: Not independently tested (no ability to restart Supabase's underlying infrastructure); durable storage is the platform's operational responsibility and covered by its documented backup/retention model (row 35).
django_justification: docker compose -f django-variant/docker-compose.yml restart (web, db and nginx) left the record count identical before and after (Section 7 hands-on check, 2026-08-15), so data survives a full container restart via the Postgres Docker volume. The absolute count at that time reflected the pre-reset dataset and is not comparable to the 2,000-row benchmark baseline, so the check is reported as an equality rather than as a figure.

criterion: Automated backups exist and are documented, with a stated retention policy
supabase_justification: Daily backups and PITR are documented platform features, but NOT included at the Free/Nano tier this project actually uses (the compute-budget decision, Section 3.3). Daily backups start at the Pro tier ($25/mo, 7-day retention); PITR is a paid add-on requiring at least a Small compute tier. At the tier actually benchmarked, no automated backup is running.
django_justification: No automated backup mechanism (cron pg_dump, VPS snapshot schedule, etc.) was configured for this reference implementation; Postgres data persists only via the Docker volume, which is not itself a backup strategy.

criterion: A documented, testable disaster-recovery/restore procedure exists
supabase_justification: Supabase publishes a general restore procedure for PITR/daily backups via the Dashboard, but no project-specific restore was actually tested during this build — and per the row above, the tier used doesn't have backups enabled to restore from in the first place.
django_justification: No disaster-recovery procedure was documented or tested for this implementation; restoring would mean manually recreating the Docker volume from a pg_dump that was never scheduled to begin with.

criterion: Uptime/SLA commitment is published (or, for self-hosted, is a function of the chosen VPS provider's published SLA)
supabase_score: Not satisfied at the tier used
supabase_justification: Supabase's 99.9% uptime SLA (supabase.com/sla) is contractually available only on the Enterprise plan (custom pricing, effectively ~$25,000+/year). Free, Pro, and Team customers have no contractual uptime commitment at all — this project runs on the Free tier, so there is no SLA in practice, only the platform's general reliability.
django_score: Not assessed — no production VPS was operated within the study window
django_justification: Formal SLA availability varies sharply by provider: DigitalOcean publishes a 99.99% SLA, Linode/Akamai offers an enterprise-grade SLA, but Hetzner publishes no formal uptime SLA at all (independently observed ~99.95%, no compensation mechanism). Score depends on which provider is actually selected in §4.11.

criterion: System exposes health-check/status endpoints suitable for external monitoring
supabase_justification: Not meaningfully testable at the application level; Supabase's own infrastructure health is monitored platform-side (status.supabase.com), not through a project-specific endpoint. Note this asymmetry rather than scoring it as a deficiency.
django_justification: Checked /health, /healthz, /api/health, /api/health/ — all returned 404. No health-check endpoint was built for this implementation; an operator would need to add one (e.g. a trivial DB-ping view) before production use.

criterion: Migration/schema-change failures are transactional (all-or-nothing, no partial schema state left behind)
supabase_justification: Postgres DDL is transactional by design; the Supabase CLI's supabase db push applies each migration file within a transaction, so a failing statement rolls back the whole file rather than leaving partial schema state.
django_justification: Django wraps each migration in an atomic transaction by default (unless a migration explicitly sets atomic = False); no partial-migration failure was encountered during this build's several makemigrations/migrate cycles.

criterion: All API endpoints require authentication by default (no accidental public exposure)
supabase_justification: Every unauthenticated request made throughout the build/test process returned 401/403; no endpoint was reachable without a valid Bearer token.
django_justification: Same — custom UserAccountJWTAuthentication + DRF permission classes reject all unauthenticated requests.

criterion: Row-level authorisation is enforced at the data layer, not only in application code
supabase_justification: RLS policies enforced directly by Postgres, independent of any application-layer code — verified by the infinite-recursion and report_view fixes, both database-level changes.
django_justification: Enforcement is at the application layer (permission classes + queryset filtering), not the Postgres layer — no RLS on the Django-managed tables. An honest architectural asymmetry worth naming directly rather than obscuring: a bug in a Django view could bypass authorisation in a way an RLS bug at the DB layer generally cannot.

criterion: Malformed or tampered JWTs are rejected with a generic error, no internal detail leaked
supabase_justification: Verified via pytest and manual curl testing across Section 5; malformed tokens return 401 without stack traces or internal detail.
django_justification: Same verification method, same result.

criterion: Expired tokens are rejected and cannot be used to authenticate further requests
supabase_justification: Encountered directly during testing — the default 1-hour Supabase token expiry caused real 401s mid-session, correctly rejected.
django_justification: Encountered directly — the default 5-minute SIMPLE_JWT access-token lifetime caused real 401s mid-session before being extended to 24h for testing convenience; expiry enforcement itself worked correctly at both settings.

criterion: Server-derived fields (e.g. created_by, org_id) cannot be overridden by client-supplied payload values
supabase_justification: Initial build allowed client-supplied created_by, enabling authorship spoofing; fixed via DB column DEFAULT auth.uid() plus a strengthened WITH CHECK policy; re-verified via pytest.
django_justification: RecordSerializer already excluded org/created_by from client input via read_only_fields; perform_create() derives both server-side.

criterion: Password storage uses a modern, salted, adaptive hashing algorithm (not reversible encryption)
supabase_justification: Supabase Auth (GoTrue) hashes passwords with bcrypt plus a per-password random salt, stored in auth.users.encrypted_password (supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/password-security).
django_justification: Django's default password hasher is PBKDF2 with SHA256 and a per-password salt — modern and adaptive (configurable work factor); this implementation did not override Django's default, and did not add django[argon2] which would be the stronger alternative if desired.

criterion: All traffic is served over TLS by default, with plaintext HTTP disabled or redirected
supabase_justification: Every request throughout this build targeted the hosted https://*.supabase.co project URL; plain HTTP is not served for the platform API.
django_justification: An nginx reverse proxy container exists in django-variant/docker-compose.yml (confirmed via row 34's restart test, 2026-08-15), but it's plain-HTTP only, no TLS certificate configured — traffic between client and nginx is still unencrypted. Real TLS termination (e.g. Let's Encrypt via certbot) was not configured within the study window, and the row is scored on the observed state: client-to-proxy traffic is unencrypted.

criterion: Sensitive configuration (API keys, DB credentials) is never present in client-side/browser-reachable code or responses
supabase_justification: Supabase's anon/publishable key is deliberately client-exposed by design (protected by RLS, not secrecy); the more privileged service_role key was never returned in any client-facing response and was only used server-side for admin API calls this session.
django_justification: SECRET_KEY, DB_PASSWORD, and other .env values live only in the container environment; no API response body observed this session ever echoed a configuration value.

criterion: Rate limiting or equivalent abuse protection exists on authentication endpoints
supabase_justification: Confirmed both by documentation (GoTrue uses a per-IP token-bucket, default capacity 30 requests — supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/rate-limits) and hands-on: a 40-request burst against the sign-in endpoint returned 400 (invalid credentials) for the first ~33 requests, then switched to 429 (Too Many Requests) for the remainder — matching the documented bucket size almost exactly.
django_justification: A 40-request burst against the real login endpoint (/token/) returned 401 on every single attempt, never 429. No rate limiting or throttling is configured on this endpoint (e.g. via django-ratelimit or DRF throttle classes).

criterion: SQL injection is not possible via any parameterised/filterable API input
supabase_justification: The direct Supabase-side probe did not complete (the test JWT expired before this check executed), so the verdict rests on architectural grounds: PostgREST compiles filter parameters into parameterised SQL and never interpolates client input into query text, foreclosing the injection class this criterion targets. The equivalent Django-side probe completed normally.
django_justification: Injection payload (?id=1' OR '1'='1) in a query filter had no effect on the executed query — Django REST Framework/ORM parameterises all queryset filtering, so the malformed param was simply not recognised as a valid filter and the endpoint fell back to its default (unfiltered) queryset rather than executing any injected SQL.

criterion: File upload endpoints reject executable/script file types by default or via explicit configuration
supabase_score: Not satisfied by default — but low-risk by architecture
supabase_justification: Supabase Storage does not restrict file types unless a bucket's allowed_mime_types is explicitly configured (an opt-in setting, not on by default). Mitigating factor: Storage objects are served as static blobs via CDN and are never executed server-side, so an uploaded .sh/.exe file poses materially less risk than the same file landing in a web-servable application directory.
django_justification: See row above — no functional upload endpoint exists in this implementation to test against.

criterion: File uploads are stored outside the web-servable document root (or equivalent isolation for object storage)
supabase_justification: Supabase Storage is dedicated object storage, architecturally isolated from any application document root by design — there is no shared filesystem between the API/Auth layer and stored objects.
django_justification: django-storages/S3Boto3Storage (as configured, albeit with placeholder credentials — see row above) stores files in object storage, not on the application server's filesystem, so isolation is correct in principle even though the credentials were never completed enough to test end-to-end.

criterion: Session/token invalidation on logout is immediate and verifiable (token cannot be reused after logout)
supabase_justification: Logout call succeeded (204), but the same access token still worked on a subsequent request (200) — the logout revokes the server-side session/refresh token, not the already-issued short-lived access token, since GoTrue JWTs are stateless and not checked against a revocation list on every request. A functioning logout endpoint exists (unlike Django), but it does not achieve immediate access-token invalidation.
django_justification: No logout/blacklist endpoint exists in this implementation; reusing the token after the client discarded it still returned 200. SIMPLE_JWT has no token-blacklist app configured, so issued tokens remain valid until natural expiry regardless of any client-side logout action. Net effect is the same as Supabase's (token survives 'logout') but for a more basic reason — no logout endpoint was built at all, vs. Supabase's endpoint existing but not covering access-token revocation.

criterion: Multi-factor authentication is available as an option for user accounts
supabase_justification: TOTP (authenticator app) and phone/SMS MFA are built into Supabase Auth and free to use on every plan including Free, via the standard Enroll/Challenge/Verify API (supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/auth-mfa). Organization-wide MFA *enforcement* requires Pro+, but the capability for a user to opt into MFA is available regardless of tier.
django_justification: No MFA was implemented in this reference implementation; adding it would require an additional package (e.g. django-otp) and is not part of djangorestframework-simplejwt out of the box.

criterion: Security-relevant events (failed logins, permission denials) are logged in a form usable for audit
supabase_justification: Failed logins and other Auth events are visible via Dashboard > Logs > Auth with event type, timestamp, and IP — a real audit trail, platform-provided.
django_justification: A deliberate failed login produced nothing in docker compose logs web (Section 7 hands-on check, 2026-08-15) — no 401/login-attempt line appeared. Caveat: this build's docker-compose.yml includes an nginx service (discovered incidentally during row 34's restart test, not previously accounted for in this catalog — see rows 37/46/86, which assumed no reverse proxy yet exists and should be re-checked against this). The failed-login request may be logged in nginx's access log rather than web's, which this check didn't inspect. Re-run against nginx logs before treating this as final.

criterion: Logs do not contain full request bodies with sensitive data (PII, credentials) by default
supabase_score: Satisfied — not independently checkable via CLI
supabase_justification: No request-body logging is exposed to the project owner via CLI on a hosted project; whatever Supabase logs server-side for its own operations isn't inspectable this way. Treated as platform-managed, not scored as a deficiency.
django_justification: Gunicorn's default access log format logs method/path/status, not request bodies — confirmed indirectly by row 3's check (a submitted password never appeared in docker compose logs web output).

criterion: CORS policy is explicit and does not default to wildcard-allow-all in a production configuration
supabase_justification: An OPTIONS preflight from an arbitrary, untrusted origin (https://evil-example.com) received access-control-allow-origin: * — wildcard by default, permitting any origin to make browser-based requests given a valid API key/token.
django_justification: The same preflight from an untrusted origin returned no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header at all — no CORS middleware is configured, so browsers block cross-origin requests by default. This technically satisfies the criterion, but it's a side effect of CORS never being configured rather than a deliberate restrictive policy; a legitimate frontend on a different origin would also be blocked and would need explicit configuration (e.g. django-cors-headers) to work at all.

criterion: Security headers (e.g. HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options) are present on API responses
supabase_justification: strict-transport-security and x-content-type-options are present by default (platform-managed). No X-Frame-Options or Content-Security-Policy header observed, though both are of limited relevance to a JSON-only API surface (no HTML rendered).
django_justification: X-Frame-Options: DENY and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff are present (Django's default SecurityMiddleware). No Strict-Transport-Security header — expected while testing over plain HTTP on localhost; would need to be verified again against a real TLS-terminated deployment (§4.11) before scoring this row as final.

criterion: Dependency/package vulnerabilities are surfaced by an available scanning mechanism (platform-provided or addable)
supabase_justification: Application code is not user-maintained (no requirements.txt/package.json for the deployed backend itself); dependency security is Supabase's operational responsibility, not something scored against a self-run scan.
django_justification: pip-audit against requirements.txt found 12 known CVEs across 3 packages: django 4.2.30 (6 CVEs, fixed in 5.2.15+/6.0.x), urllib3 1.26.20 (5 CVEs, fixed in 2.5.0-2.7.0), python-dotenv 1.2.1 (1 CVE, fixed in 1.2.2). The scanning mechanism itself is satisfied — it's available, free, and worked — but the findings are a real, disclosed limitation: dependencies should be bumped before final submission/production use.

criterion: Business-logic constraints (e.g. a record cannot belong to two organisations) are enforced server-side, not just in the client
supabase_justification: org_id is server-derived (see created_by row above) and RLS additionally scopes every query; a record cannot be associated with an org the caller doesn't belong to.
django_justification: org is server-derived via perform_create() and get_queryset() filtering; same guarantee enforced server-side.

criterion: Administrative/privileged operations require a distinct, more strongly authenticated credential than standard user operations
supabase_justification: The Admin API (used this session for direct password resets) requires the service_role key, a distinct, more privileged credential than a regular user's JWT — confirmed hands-on when performing user-management operations.
django_justification: This application's API uses the same UserAccountJWTAuthentication scheme for every endpoint; no separate elevated-privilege authentication path exists (Django's built-in admin site, which uses session auth, was never registered/used for these models).

criterion: Input length/size limits are enforced to prevent resource-exhaustion via oversized payloads
supabase_justification: POST with a 500,000-character string in the title field was rejected (400) rather than accepted — the underlying Postgres column type/constraint enforces a limit.
django_justification: POST with a 500,000-character string in a text field returned 201 Created with no rejection or truncation — no field-level or request-level size limit is enforced.

criterion: Direct object references (e.g. record IDs) cannot be enumerated to access other organisations' data
supabase_justification: Explicitly covered by the cross-org record ID tests in test_authorization.py (OTHER_ORG_RECORD_ID fixture), 12/12 passing — a known other-org record ID returns 200+[] (empty), not the record.
django_justification: Same test suite, same fixture — a known other-org record ID returns 404, not the record.

criterion: Secrets rotation (API keys, DB passwords) is possible without downtime
supabase_justification: This project's Supabase instance uses the newer asymmetric API-key/signing-key system (confirmed via the dashboard's JWT Signing Keys UI encountered earlier in this build). Under that system, publishable and secret keys can be rotated instantly without invalidating existing user sessions. (Note: the legacy shared-secret JWT system, still in use by older Supabase projects, does NOT support this — regenerating the JWT secret there immediately invalidates all issued keys/sessions.)
django_justification: Rotating DB_PASSWORD means updating django-variant/.env and restarting the web/db containers — a brief service interruption in this simple docker-compose setup, since there's no rolling-restart or connection-draining mechanism configured. A production setup would need multiple replicas or a managed DB to avoid this.

criterion: Threat-modelling or security-architecture documentation is available for the platform's own infrastructure (BaaS) or was produced for this deployment (self-hosted)
supabase_justification: Supabase publishes general platform security/compliance documentation, but no project-specific threat model was produced for this deployment beyond the ad-hoc findings logged during the build (RLS recursion, view security_invoker, authorship spoofing).
django_justification: No formal threat-modelling document was produced for this deployment either, but the same ad-hoc security findings during the build (server-derived fields, RLS-layer absence noted at row 41) functionally constitute informal threat analysis, even though it wasn't organised as a structured document (e.g. STRIDE).

criterion: Codebase is organised into clearly separable modules/layers (data access, business logic, API surface)
supabase_score: N/A — architecturally different, not a deficiency
supabase_justification: Business logic lives as SQL migrations + RLS policies (row 74); there is no separate data-access/business-logic/API-surface split in the traditional sense because PostgREST generates the API surface automatically from the schema. Not comparable to Django's layering on a like-for-like basis.
django_justification: core/ follows the conventional DRF layout — models.py, serializers.py, views.py, urls.py as separate files/concerns, confirmed via grep this session (core/urls.py, core/views.py, core/models.py referenced independently).

criterion: A change to one endpoint's validation logic does not require touching unrelated modules
supabase_justification: RLS policies are per-table, so changing one table's validation rule (a WITH CHECK clause) doesn't touch other tables' policies. But policies for the same table are coupled together in one CREATE POLICY statement per operation, so a validation change can require re-reasoning about the whole policy, not just one isolated rule (seen directly in the created_by fix, which touched both a column default and a WITH CHECK clause together).
django_justification: DRF's per-view/per-serializer structure means validation for one endpoint (a serializer's validate() method or a permission class) is isolated from other endpoints' files; the created_by fix (row 44) only touched RecordSerializer's read_only_fields, nothing else.

criterion: Automated test suite exists and covers the core authorisation logic
assessment_method: Hands-on verification (Section 5, this guide's own test suite)
supabase_justification: 12 cross-target integration tests (test_authorization.py + test_equivalence.py) exercise RLS and permission boundaries directly; all passing.
django_justification: Same 12 integration tests plus 4 Django-specific unit tests; all passing.

criterion: Test suite can be run in a single command with no manual setup beyond documented steps
supabase_justification: pytest tests/ (with tests/config.py sourcing .env) runs the full cross-target suite in one command.
django_justification: Same command for integration tests; docker compose run --rm web pytest for the Django-specific unit tests.

criterion: Static analysis / linting is configured and passes cleanly
supabase_justification: The Supabase variant has no application-layer code to lint in the conventional sense (Python/JS linters don't apply) — just SQL migrations and shell scripts. Not scored against Django on this row; noted as an architectural asymmetry rather than a deficiency.
django_justification: ruff (a standard, widely-used Python linter) runs cleanly against the codebase but reports 32 issues, 19 auto-fixable (mostly import ordering, not serious defects). Linting is available and works, but the codebase doesn't yet pass cleanly — would take a five-minute `ruff check --fix` pass before final submission.

criterion: Code changes can be reviewed via a standard diff (not exclusively through a proprietary dashboard UI)
supabase_justification: Schema/RLS migrations are plain SQL, fully diffable in git. Auth and Storage configuration changes made via the dashboard (same gap as row 71) are not diffable — they'd need to be reconstructed as a change description, not a git diff.
django_justification: All business logic is plain Python source under version control; every change this session was reviewable as a standard git diff.

criterion: Business logic that would traditionally live in Edge Functions/serverless functions is inspectable and version-controllable as plain source, not only configured through a dashboard
supabase_justification: No Edge Functions were built for this implementation (RLS was judged sufficient for this application's business logic). RLS policies themselves are version-controlled SQL migrations, but Auth/Storage configuration was done via the dashboard, not fully expressed as code.
django_justification: All business logic is plain Python under version control; no dashboard-only configuration path exists for application logic.

criterion: A new developer can trace a request from API entry point to database query without needing platform-specific internal knowledge
supabase_justification: Tracing a request means understanding PostgREST's automatic table-to-endpoint mapping and how RLS evaluates against auth.uid() at query time — Postgres/PostgREST-specific knowledge, not general web-development knowledge.
django_justification: Fully traceable by anyone familiar with Django/DRF conventions: urls.py to views.py to serializers.py to models.py, all plain Python, no platform-proprietary internals.

criterion: Lines of code and dependency count are known and documented for the implementation (Section 5.4/Table 5.4)
supabase_justification: 204 LOC (cloc), 8 deployment steps (§3, awk step count) — documented in Table 5.4 (Section 9).
django_justification: 343 LOC (cloc), 15 deployment steps (§4, awk step count), 23 dependencies (requirements.txt) — documented in Table 5.4 (Section 9).

criterion: Database schema changes are tracked in version control as migrations, not only as live dashboard edits
supabase_justification: Initial schema was migration-tracked (0001-0003), but several fixes this session (RLS recursion fix, security_invoker view fix, created_by default) were applied live via the SQL Editor rather than committed migration files. These fixes have since been committed as migration 0004_fixes.sql (Appendix A), restoring a complete migration chain; the Partial score reflects the state during the assessed build window, when the live database and the committed migrations diverged.
django_justification: All schema changes went through makemigrations/migrate and are fully tracked in version control.

criterion: Test coverage percentage is measurable and reported
supabase_justification: No conventional code-coverage metric applies — there's no application code to instrument (same architectural asymmetry as row 69). The 12 cross-target integration tests exercise Supabase-side behaviour functionally, but not as a coverage percentage.
django_justification: pytest-cov measured 38% total statement coverage this session (--ds=config.settings run against core/tests.py, Section 9), with per-file percentages reported.

criterion: Application can run against a different underlying Postgres provider (self-hosted, different cloud) without code changes
supabase_justification: PostgREST, GoTrue, and Storage are each individually open-source and self-hostable against any Postgres instance, so the underlying stack can in principle run elsewhere. But 'Supabase' as the managed platform used in this build does not itself run against a different provider — realizing this portability means self-hosting those OSS components, a materially bigger step than a config change.
django_justification: Vanilla postgres:16, no extensions (row 81); pointing at a different provider is a one-line change to the DATABASES setting in settings.py, no code changes required.

criterion: Full data export (schema + data) is possible in a standard format (e.g. pg_dump) without provider-specific tooling
supabase_justification: Both variants are plain PostgreSQL databases; pg_dump works identically against either. Supabase also exposes a direct Postgres connection string for this purpose (Settings > Database), not requiring the Supabase CLI.
django_justification: Same — django-variant's db container is unmodified postgres:16; pg_dump requires no Django-specific tooling.

criterion: Application container/runtime can be installed on a fresh environment following only the documented steps in this guide
supabase_justification: Platform_Build_Guide.md was executed step by step across this build; every genuine gap found along the way (Gunicorn worker sizing, the zsh array word-splitting bug in §6, missing pytest install, missing --ds flag, JWT-refresh flow) was folded back into the guide itself as it was discovered, so the current version reflects a verified-working path.
django_justification: Same guide, same verification process — the Django-variant sections were patched in step with the same issues as they came up (Gunicorn worker count, k6 loop, pytest/coverage setup).

criterion: Switching to a different auth provider is possible without a full application rewrite
supabase_justification: Supabase publishes official migration guides for Auth0, AWS Cognito, and Firebase Auth, and supports running Supabase Auth alongside a third-party provider during migration to avoid disruption. Supabase Auth (GoTrue) is itself open-source and self-hostable, which further reduces lock-in risk.
django_justification: Authentication is a thin, explicitly custom layer (UserAccountJWTAuthentication + djangorestframework-simplejwt); swapping to a different provider means replacing one authentication backend class, not a framework-level rewrite.

criterion: Switching to a different object-storage backend is possible without a full application rewrite
supabase_justification: Supabase Storage exposes an S3-compatible API, so the underlying files/buckets can be moved to another S3-compatible provider — but the storage.objects metadata table, its RLS policies, and any Supabase-Storage-specific client calls are platform-specific and would need to be rebuilt against the new backend, not just re-pointed.
django_justification: django-storages (S3Boto3Storage, configured in §4.6) already abstracts the storage backend behind Django's standard storage API; swapping providers (or backend type entirely — filesystem, GCS, Azure) is a settings.py configuration change, not a code rewrite.

criterion: No proprietary, non-standard SQL extensions are required for the application's core schema/queries to function
supabase_justification: Row-Level Security (SECURITY DEFINER functions, RLS policies) is a standard PostgreSQL 9.5+ feature, not a Supabase-proprietary extension — the schema would run unmodified on any plain Postgres instance.
django_justification: No extensions used beyond core PostgreSQL/Django ORM features.

criterion: Local development environment can be run entirely offline/without a live cloud account (self-hosted) vs. requires live cloud connectivity (BaaS) — document this asymmetry, don't score it as a deficiency for either side
supabase_justification: Every request throughout this build targeted a hosted https://*.supabase.co project; no offline/local-emulation mode was used. Requires live cloud connectivity by design.
django_justification: Runs entirely offline once Docker images are pulled — confirmed throughout this session, docker compose up brings up web+db locally with no external network dependency for normal operation.

criterion: Vendor lock-in risk is explicitly assessable: estimated effort (hours) to migrate away from the current provider/stack
supabase_justification: Migrating away means either self-hosting the OSS components (PostgREST/GoTrue/Storage, row 76) or rewriting Auth and RLS as application-layer logic against a different BaaS/framework — the RLS policies alone (row 41) would need to become explicit Python authorization code with no direct 1:1 translation.
django_justification: Mostly an infrastructure/redeploy exercise since the stack is already vanilla Postgres+Django (row 76): provision a new VPS, restore via pg_dump (row 77), redeploy the existing Docker containers. No application code would need to change.

criterion: Time from zero to a working authenticated CRUD endpoint (first successful request) is measured and documented
assessment_method: Hands-on, self-reported (from this guide's own build timeline)
supabase_justification: Not formally time-boxed; self-reported that Django reached its first working authenticated CRUD request sooner than Supabase, despite Supabase's smaller final codebase (row 73) — consistent with the RLS recursion fix blocking a working request until resolved.
django_justification: Not formally time-boxed; self-reported as reaching the first working authenticated CRUD request faster than Supabase, since the initial Django CRUD path didn't hit a comparable correctness blocker before its first successful request.

criterion: Number of discrete manual dashboard/console configuration steps required (vs. steps expressible as code/CLI)
supabase_justification: Self-reported: roughly 3-4 of the 8 §3 deployment steps required the dashboard/console (e.g. project creation, retrieving API keys, storage bucket setup), with the rest (schema, RLS policies, auth trigger) expressed as SQL migrations run via CLI.
django_justification: All 15 §4 deployment steps are CLI commands or file edits (Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, .env, manage.py commands); no dashboard/console exists for this self-hosted variant.

criterion: Number of distinct services/processes an operator is responsible for keeping running (self-hosted) vs. zero (BaaS)
supabase_justification: Fully managed — zero processes for the operator to keep running (Postgres, API layer, Auth, Storage are all Supabase's operational responsibility).
django_justification: web, db, and nginx containers in the current docker-compose.yml (nginx confirmed via row 34's restart test, 2026-08-15). Note this corrects an earlier assumption in this catalog that nginx hadn't been added yet — it has, but as a plain-HTTP reverse proxy without TLS configured (row 46).

criterion: Monthly direct cost at each of the three usage scenarios in Table 3.3 is known and documented
supabase_justification: $35/$40/$135 for small/growing/peak, confirmed against a dated (2026-08-15) pricing-page screenshot — see Table 5.3 and Appendix C.
django_justification: $11.99/$14.99/$28.99 (Hostinger renewal rate) for small/growing/peak, confirmed against the same dated screenshot — see Table 5.3 and Appendix C.

criterion: Overage/scaling cost behaviour beyond the base tier is documented (linear, stepped, or unpredictable)
supabase_justification: Overage is per-resource metered at published per-unit rates beyond each plan's included allowance: database storage $0.125/GB, egress $0.09/GB beyond 250GB included, file storage $0.021/GB, and $0.00325 per monthly active user. Predictable and linear, but egress and MAU are the two meters most likely to surprise a growing app, since both scale with usage rather than storage.
django_justification: VPS pricing is flat/fixed per compute tier (e.g. DigitalOcean/Hetzner/Linode droplet pricing), not usage-metered — cost is a step function of the chosen tier rather than a continuous function of load, until bandwidth caps are exceeded (typically generous, several TB included per most providers). This fixed-vs-metered distinction is itself a core TCO finding for Table 5.3, not just a documentation note.

criterion: Estimated monthly operational effort (hours) for patching, monitoring, and backups is documented
supabase_justification: ~1 hr/month (occasional dashboard checks, no patching/backup management) — operational-effort estimate, Section 3.5.
django_justification: ~4-8 hrs/month (OS patching, container updates, backup verification, monitoring), scaling up somewhat at the peak scenario — operational-effort estimate, Section 3.5.
